Over the past several weeks, teams across Google and academic partner institutions have tackled open problems in math, science, and complex systems engineering that had remained open for years. Using Gemini 4 Argon, Gemini 4 Carbon, Gemini 4 Hydrogen and multi-agent workflows such as Antigravity’s /teamwork (building on various Gemini models), these collaborations have produced new innovations across information theory, formal verifications, molecular structure discoveries, and kernel optimization, along with several production infrastructure gains at Google. We are making these agentic tools available in Antigravity’s /teamwork (alongside /boost and other agents) so that researchers and developers can apply them to their own work.

Frontier research and systems engineering require navigating vast literature, building custom computational pipelines, testing against physical measurements, and verifying every step. Progress comes from an interactive discovery loop where researchers frame questions and define the theoretical or physical constraints, while long-horizon agents write custom solvers, explore large search spaces, test candidate designs, and check long chains of logic.

Scaling long-horizon reasoning

Two limits of current language models motivate /teamwork's design. First, model generation can be unpredictable, leaving a gap between a single attempt and finding the correct answer. The system bridges this gap by pairing parallel exploration with dedicated falsifiers (e.g., the Lean 4 proof checker, unmodified software test suites, execution simulators, web search, or hardware counters) to automatically verify which candidate solutions work.

Second, AI models often lose track of details over multi-day tasks because attention disperses across growing context windows. To prevent this, /teamwork partitions context by construction: each specialized agent receives only the exact files and tools it needs for a specific step. Coordinators hand off tasks to fresh successors, while critics and auditors challenge and verify results from clean contexts without the original producer's reasoning.

Teamwork expresses these workflows as declarative self-improving natural-language patterns and dynamically routes each user prompt to the pattern best suited to the task. These patterns range from distributed coding and iterative problem-solving (packaged standalone as /boost, a sequential solve-and-verify loop refined from prior trajectories) to specialized research workflows like long proof and document review, all of which are available in Antigravity today. This allows teams to design custom specifications from past run transcripts routing across different harness patterns and dynamically improving agentic harness. While many of these features are available in Antigravity, we will provide more updates in the coming weeks providing all the features to our external users on Antigravity. Following our previous posts on Antigravity /teamwork, we provide new results to open challenges empowered by new variants of /teamwork and Gemini 4 models.

Mathematics and theoretical computer science

Across mathematics and theoretical computer science, researchers paired with Gemini 4 and /teamwork harnesses to collaborate on large-scale proofs and generate complete algorithms and proofs directly from open problem statements. We present several examples.

Proving and verifying the Courtade–Kumar conjecture

Researchers from Google, CUHK, USC, and CMU used /teamwork's Long Proof pattern (implementing Stellar Colosseum in Antigravity) to prove information theory's 2013 Courtade–Kumar conjecture in full generality. The result confirms that when a random bit string passes through a noisy channel, no compression of the input to a single bit preserves more information than a "dictator function", which just copies a single input bit. Gemini first found counterexamples to a generalized conjecture from the CUHK team's earlier paper. The CUHK team then proposed a new candidate function that reduced the conjecture to a 14-variable optimization problem, along with a key analytical lower bound. Gemini 4 Argon and earlier Gemini models then partitioned the parameter space and developed most of the new analytical bounds and interval-arithmetic certificates. They also extended the proof from balanced to unbalanced functions without human input. The team formalized the entire proof in Lean 4, producing 50 million lines of code.

Resolving open questions in optimization, statistics, quantum computing, and algorithms

Researchers also posed open problems directly to Gemini 4 and to multi-agent harnesses such as Stellar Colosseum and /teamwork, receiving end-to-end algorithms and proofs (often with Lean 4 formalizations) that the authors verified, simplified, and edited for publication. In adaptive data analysis, a multi-agent harness running on Gemini 4 Argon independently proved and Lean-verified near-optimal sample bounds for statistical queries chosen adaptively from earlier answers, closing a gap open since 2014. These bounds yield the first nearly space-optimal algorithm for data streams with both insertions and deletions that stays accurate against adaptive adversaries. In quantum computing, a new construction settled a 2014 open question by finding the first n-bit Boolean functions needing strictly more than n/2 quantum queries at constant error, while pinning down the exact query overhead across symmetric functions.

Several results break long standing barriers in processing and compressing large matrices and graphs. For fifty years until STOC 2024, combinatorial algorithms for Boolean matrix multiplication and triangle detection (avoiding the algebraic cancellations of fast matrix multiplication) saved only logarithmic factors over cubic time. A new deterministic algorithm resolves STOC 2024's main open question, achieving its target speedup over cubic time. In high-dimensional geometry, a new lower bound resolves an open problem on sparse networks, proving that approximating all pairwise distances among n points within any constant factor can require polynomially more than n edges, even with extra Steiner points and arbitrarily many hops. In randomized linear algebra, stacked sparse sketches resolve a 2025 open question by breaking the classical sparsity barrier for compressing a matrix to linear dimension without collapsing any direction of an r-dimensional subspace, needing only √log r nonzeros per row (quadratically fewer than the log r required to preserve all lengths) and nearly matching a new lower bound. For weighted graphs under dynamic edge-weight insertions and deletions, Stellar Colosseum resolved an open question left by FOCS 2022, developing the first single-pass streaming algorithm for cut sparsification that achieves near-optimal memory, update time, and reconstruction time simultaneously.

Our results also span optimization, arithmetic, data structures, and statistics. In optimization, resolving an open question on online inverse linear optimization (inferring an expert's hidden objective from decisions over time), the approach gave a deterministic algorithm achieving optimal regret while cutting runtime from exponential in the dimension to polynomial time. For n-bit integer multiplication, multi-agent campaigns simplified the theoretical Turing-machine bound below n log n, while a separate effort gave a new O(n log n) algorithm on a single two-dimensional grid whose C implementation matches the GNU Multiple Precision Arithmetic Library (GMP) bit-for-bit up to a billion bits. In data structures, another result made significant progress on Tarjan's 1985 Deque Conjecture (whether self-adjusting splay trees handle insertions and deletions at both ends in constant amortized time), proving a new upper bound on the per-operation overhead that simultaneously beats every finitely iterated inverse-Ackermann function, verified in Lean 4. Finally, in high-dimensional statistics, the approach proved that approximate leave-one-out cross-validation, which avoids refitting the model from scratch, remains accurate for non-smooth sparse penalties like elastic net.

Scaling formal verification and manuscript review

Checking a computer-assisted manuscript by hand places a heavy burden on peer reviewers, and subtle flaws can hide inside long calculations. Formalizing mathematics in Lean 4 turns a proof into code that a computer kernel checks line by line. Once human mathematicians confirm that the formal theorem statement matches the original problem, the proof only compiles if every logical step holds.

Many of the deepest open problems in mathematics govern how physical waves propagate, how dynamical systems evolve, and whether polynomial equations have integer solutions. Working directly from informal proofs, our multi-agent framework, LEAP, developed with colleagues in Google Cloud AI and paired with Argon, has made progress in these core areas.

Notably, /teamwork-LEAP fully autonomously produced an end-to-end, machine-checked formalization of the Weil conjectures, the landmark results on counting solutions of polynomial equations over finite fields that culminated in Pierre Deligne's 1974 proof. This formalization spans about 1.8 million lines of Lean, produced across 28,800 subagent invocations. The system also synthesized over 919,000 lines of Lean to produce the first formalization of a recent proof of Hilbert's tenth problem over general rings of integers. It also independently reproduces an end-to-end formalization of a recent proof of finite-time blowup for the 3D Navier–Stokes equations with smooth forcing, part of one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems and open for about 90 years.

Beyond these, it also generated the first formalization of the Birkhoff conjecture, a dynamical-systems problem open since 1927. Moreover, it formalized for the first time the 3D Bochner–Riesz conjecture, a central problem in harmonic analysis open for more than 50 years, finding and fixing a gap in a recently released informal proof along the way. Additional machine-checked breakthroughs include resolving the C¹ regularity of infinity-harmonic functions in three and higher dimensions (an open question for about 20 years), formalizing Killip and Vişan's theorem that the KdV water-wave equation is well-posed in H⁻¹ and verifying a UCLA group's informal proofs of the 40-year-old Jamison Caterpillar Conjecture, the Ağırseven-Ollis conjecture, and an improved upper bound on Erdős Problem #1063.

Finally, we provided Deep Review for authors of another CS conference: ahead of STOC 2027, authors of 578 submissions (over a third of all submissions) opted in to receive Deep Review feedback on their drafts. In an ongoing author survey (N = 70), 90% of respondents rated the feedback mostly or almost all factual and 90% said they would use the tool again. Over 30% said Deep Review caught substantive proof bugs or mathematically significant typos, and 14% said it found technical gaps that took more than an hour to fix. Surveyed authors shared that “Tools of this kind can help produce cleaner and more precise research, faster” and that DeepReview provides peace of mind on scientific discovery”. We provide users two weekly calls to Deep Review for free. Deep Review is also implemented as /teamwork's document review pattern and available in Antigravity. Read more about DeepReview in our recent blog post.

Molecular chemistry discovery

Beyond formal proofs, pairing specialized generator agents with independent verifier agents enables discovery workflows in experimental laboratory science.

Determining a molecule’s structure from experimental nuclear magnetic resonance data is one of chemistry’s hardest puzzles. For example, in HIV protease inhibitors, one misplaced bond separates an inactive look-alike from a drug. By organizing 30 specialized agents into a self-correcting loop with /teamwork and a physics-informed spectral simulator, we achieved 95% top-1 exact match and 100% top-3 accuracy on complex benchmark molecules, nearly doubling single-agent performance. Beyond teaching Gemini to reason over structure, this lays the groundwork for ongoing works on 3D protein and complex structures dynamics.

Beyond this example, science problems including applications in nuclear fusion and quantum algorithms reported in the Gemini 4 blog post benefited from /teamwork and the Argon model.

Generating a causal inference benchmark

We also applied a similar multi-round auditing workflow to build empirical benchmarks. Starting from five human-specified acceptance criteria like data anonymization, 29 agents running on Argon over 11.5 hours turned 13 public tables into a 50-task causal inference benchmark. In these tasks, models must determine whether a causal effect can be identified and estimate it against a known answer. After initial checks, separate reviewer and auditor agents caught shortcuts, flagged wording hints, and vetoed hallucinated scripts, turning each into a permanent test. Automating this heavily manual task generation supplies the hard problems needed to help Gemini answer counterfactual "what-if" questions.

Coding and systems engineering

When paired with objective evaluators such as network benchmarks, game engines, unmodified test suites, and hardware timers, /teamwork campaigns can execute multi-day software and hardware engineering projects.

Distributed systems

Using /teamwork and Argon, we built FarArray, a low-latency kernel-bypass Partitioned Global Address Space based on the SNAP microkernel. Applications built on FarArray include lock-free Connected Components, which scale to 1-trillion-edge graphs with 60x to 90x throughput gains and 40x to 180x speedups at 6x lower RAM over TCP key-value stores. Similarly, InstantEmbedding (Personalized PageRank) reduced peak DRAM by up to 14x and runtime by 11x to 27x over accelerated MapReduce implementations. The team also used /teamwork and Argon to create custom TPU kernels for Graph Neural Networks, delivering up to a 185x High Bandwidth Memory reduction and 8x to 15x speedups in forward and backward passes. Further details are available in our recent Antigravity blog post.

Autonomous hill climbing

To test autonomous optimization over long horizons, hill-climbing teams on Argon trained a 9x9 Go engine from scratch starting from a basic AlphaZero implementation. Human researchers set the chip allocation and evaluation setup, while the harness ran autonomous campaigns for faster self-play (achieving a 2,300x speedup) and faster Elo readings, promoting champions strictly via statistical tests on locked records. In under eight days, the engine gained roughly 2,600 Elo, reaching 1,885 Elo, placing it between KataGo at 16 and 32 visits per move.

Memory-safe Rust rewrites, /boost, and TPU kernel optimization

Large code migrations fail when agents stub out dependencies or alter tests to make a broken port pass. A new /teamwork rewrite pattern, soon to be available in Antigravity, solved this by scheduling each module only after its dependencies compile, linking every leaf module against the original, unmodified test suite. Building on the initial 25% port of the Zircon microkernel, a two-week Argon campaign rewrote the remaining C++ code, adding about 800,000 lines of safe Rust that pass all kernel unit tests and boot on arm64 hardware. /teamwork also rewrote libgav1, Google's AV1 video decoder, from C++ into around 170k lines Rust, achieving 100% bit-exact parity across a broad conformance test suite. Initially, the port was around 4x slower than the original C++ code. However, after giving /teamwork access to profiling tools and a mandate to maximize speed on sample video clips, the Rust port became 20-30% faster than the original C++ and hand-optimized assembly code on both x86_64 and ARM.

For day-to-day coding tasks, the Antigravity /boost command packages /teamwork's iterative coding pattern. A long-running /teamwork campaign analyzed past run trajectories and found that tightly coupled code is best handled through sequential implementation and revision stages rather than parallel splits, improving /boost on coding tasks. This is an example of a harness optimizing another harness for token efficiency.

For machine learning systems, full hardware evaluations of custom JAX and Pallas TPU kernels take 7 to 32 minutes, limiting how many candidates prior optimization agents can explore. Using /teamwork's DuoDiscover pattern on Argon, four parallel agents identified performance bottlenecks and constructed fast, 23-second proxy evaluators called yardsticks. These yardsticks produce candidate orderings that are continuously validated against periodic full hardware runs using Kendall's rank correlation. DuoDiscover achieves a 4.09x geometric-mean speedup over reference implementations across 17 JAXBench kernels and a 2.99x geometric-mean speedup across 7 hand-optimized vLLM TPU-Inference Pallas kernels for frontier open-weight models.

Google infrastructure applications

We have also applied /teamwork and /boost to many production infrastructure and hardware modeling problems across Google. Examples include:

  • Fleet-wide memory optimization: Building on the initial Argon memory efforts, we analyzed fleet-wide metrics, as well as internal memory saving past successes, and created reusable /teamwork workflows that have identified memory saving opportunities, surpassing our initial savings estimates of 1 PiB. We also deployed the human-in-the-loop Memory Efficiency Monitoring Agent, achieving additional memory savings, using techniques such as struct padding elimination, scalar narrowing, cliff jumping, outlining, and tagged pointers.
  • Borg agentic scheduling: Built on /teamwork and /boost, Borg’s agentic workflow for scheduling optimization shipped 2 successful changes, resulting in a 24% reduction in TPU workload preemption on some hardware types, while preserving workload SLOs and cluster utilization.

Opening these tools to the research and developer community

External scientists and developers can use Gemini 4 models with /teamwork and /boost in Antigravity and Deep Review today. We have also opened applications giving 10,000 academic researchers six months of free access to our highest usage tier. Upcoming updates will bring our formal proof pattern and additional specialized workflows into Antigravity. These features will be accompanied by deep-dive tutorials on the Antigravity blog in the coming weeks, ensuring that developers and researchers have the resources needed to generate, inspect, and iteratively refine custom multi-agent teams. We are excited to make our tools (in addition to our models) available for everyone.

Heart disease, kidney conditions, and metabolic disorders like type 2 diabetes aren't isolated, they form an interconnected web known as cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome. CKM progression often begins silently years before symptoms appear, shaped by everyday habits like movement, sleep, and cardiovascular activity. Catching these subtle shifts early offers the best chance to reverse the trend. Yet while smartwatches easily track what we did yesterday, moving from passive tracking to meaningful action is much harder: How do my daily habits affect my CKM right now? And if I sleep 30 minutes longer or add a brisk walk to my routine, how much will my health improve over the next three months?

Age is often seen as playing a part in answering these questions, but chronological age alone isn’t enough because two people born in the same year can have vastly different physiological health. While researchers have developed “biological clocks” from blood tests or wearable sensors to estimate whether someone's body is aging faster or slower than their calendar age, most existing clocks aren't built for everyday coaching. Many are trained simply to estimate the birth year, latching onto traits you can't easily change, or act as black boxes that can't show how modifying a specific habit will shift your future health.

In “Personalized health coaching via coachable health age and counterfactual wearable trajectories” and our companion study, “Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Health Age Using Wearables and Blood Biomarkers”, we introduce an investigational framework designed to close the loop between tracking a person’s health and actively improving it. The framework provides the following:

  1. A coachable health age model: An interpretable health-age metric built entirely from modifiable daily behaviors and physiology captured passively by consumer wearables.
  2. A sensor world model and counterfactual coaching system: A machine learning world model (SensorWM) trained on over 2.2 million person-weeks of wearable data that simulates personalized 12-week "what-if" health trajectories, paired with a language model agent that turns those simulations into realistic, clinician-vetted coaching plans.
  3. Expansion to multi-organ CKM health: When routine blood tests are available, our framework can be expanded to combine wearable streams with lab biomarkers to detect early, subclinical strain across the heart, kidney, and metabolic systems.

Overview of our framework, from estimating coachable health age and predicting long-term disease risk to simulating 12-week "what-if" habit trajectories for personalized coaching.

A health age metric you can actually move

To make a health metric useful for coaching, every input should be something that can be tracked continuously and influenced through daily choices. Rather than training a model to guess a person’s birth year, we grounded our coachable health age (CHA) model in published epidemiological studies linking everyday behaviors to cardio-metabolic disease risk. CHA integrates four core signals passively measured by consumer wearables — resting heart rate, daily step count, sleep duration, and weekly Active Zone Minutes — alongside optional markers like VO2max, sleep schedule regularity, and insulin resistance, when available. Because active people often have lower resting heart rates and better sleep, we mathematically adjust for overlap across these signals so each habit contributes its distinct share to your health age delta, the difference between your CHA and chronological age. A negative delta (say, −3 years) means an individual's physiological profile appears younger than their chronological age, while a positive delta signals accelerated aging.

We validated this model across three independent cohorts:

  • Predicting future disease (All of Us research program, n = 22,748): Across more than 68,000 person-years of consenting Fitbit and electronic health record follow-up, healthy participants who had a health age older than their calendar age at baseline were significantly more likely to develop hypertension, cardiovascular disease, or type 2 diabetes over the next eight years. Adding CHA to standard clinical metrics (age, sex, and BMI) significantly improved disease risk prediction, especially among adults under 50.
  • Improvement over time (longitudinal Fitbit cohort, n = 1,464): Tracking users across consecutive 3-month windows over two years showed that among users with a sustained change in habits, the CHA decreased.
  • Alignment with clinical health (WEAR-ME study): Unlike wearable aging clocks trained to predict chronological age, CHA aligned better with the modified American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 cardiovascular score and metabolic syndrome severity score, as well as participants' own self-reported health.

Across 18,423 disease-free participants in the All of Us cohort, those with a health age younger than or equal to their calendar age had significantly higher disease-free survival over 8 years (left), while 2-year longitudinal tracking shows that individuals can meaningfully lower their health age over 3-month windows (right).

Playing out "what-if" futures with a sensor world model

Knowing your health age tells you where you stand today. Turning that number into a personalized plan requires answering a "what-if" (or counterfactual) question: What will happen to my body over the next 12 weeks if I change specific habits, and which plan can I realistically stick with?

Simply plugging new step or sleep targets into a static calculator misses how the body adapts as a connected system. When you consistently move more and sleep better over several weeks, your resting heart rate and heart rate variability gradually improve too, creating extra health benefits downstream.

To capture these dynamics, we developed Sensor World Model (SensorWM), an action-conditioned world model pre-trained on 2.28 million person-weeks of de-identified data from roughly 100,000 consenting Fitbit users. Given two weeks of baseline wearable data, SensorWM forecasts how 20 physiological markers will evolve over the next 12 weeks under different daily steps, sleep, and cardio routines, outperforming general-purpose time-series foundation models like TimesFM while preserving the clinical patterns associated with diabetes, hypertension, and insulin resistance.

We paired SensorWM with a feasibility-constrained optimizer and a language model coaching agent to do three things:

  1. Simulate: SensorWM rolls out 125 candidate 12-week habit combinations for each person, comparing them against a "status-quo" projection if habits stay the same.
  2. Filter for realism and safety: The most aggressive workout plan doesn't help if it causes burnout in week two. Our optimizer weighs projected health-age reductions against each person's historical habit flexibility and clinical safety bounds, picking a more ambitious target (−2.3 years) for someone with high baseline flexibility, and a gentler ramp (−1.3 years) for someone whose routine is more constrained.
  3. Coach: The language model translates the top-ranked pathways into a supportive, progressive 12-week coaching plan.

SensorWM simulates 12-week physiological responses under candidate habit changes and balances health-age improvement against each person's historical habit flexibility.

Put to the test by lifestyle coaches and clinicians

Does grounding a language model in world-model simulations actually produce better guidance than giving the exact same model a user's wearable history alone?

We ran a blinded, head-to-head study with five certified lifestyle coaches and five board-certified primary care and lifestyle medicine physicians across 49 participant profiles spanning five behavioral personas (490 paired reviews total), alongside automated evaluations across the full WEAR-ME cohort (n = 2,780).

  • Strong expert preference: Lifestyle coaches chose the counterfactual-grounded plan as the best overall plan in 71.4% of evaluations (p < 0.001) and rated it more likely to drive long-term adherence in 71.0% of evaluations (p < 0.001).
  • Clinician-verified safety: Physicians rated 99.2% of counterfactual plans within safe exercise intensity limits and 97.6% accurate on physiological claims.
  • Why it worked: Both coaches and clinicians highlighted that showing people a concrete contrast between their "status-quo" trajectory and achievable "what-if" options (92% vs. 8% among clinicians) gave them a clear, motivating reason to act and a stronger sense of agency (97% vs. 59%).

In blinded evaluations by certified lifestyle coaches and board-certified clinicians, counterfactual-grounded coaching plans were preferred nearly 3-to-1 over generic wearable-grounded plans while meeting 99.2% clinical safety standards.

Zooming in on organ systems: Adding routine blood biomarkers for CKM health

Because our health age model is modular, it can easily incorporate routine clinical lab tests when available. In our companion study, we expanded the framework to profile CKM syndrome across individual organ systems, pairing continuous wearables with occasional blood biomarkers that alone miss day to day lifestyle patterns.

Conceptual framework of the multimodal CKM health age model, integrating wearable physiology with organ-specific blood biomarkers across diverse aging profiles.

Early CKM decline rarely causes symptoms, and occasional clinic blood draws miss day-to-day lifestyle patterns. Evaluated in 819 WEAR-ME participants, our multimodal CKM health age model combines continuous wearable signals (resting heart rate, steps, active zone minutes, and sleep) with three routine blood biomarkers: cholesterol-to-HDL ratio (cardiovascular), eGFR (kidney filtration), and HOMA-IR (metabolic insulin resistance).

By measuring how far each marker departs from healthy clinical thresholds (a normalized deviance score), the CKM model revealed that multi-organ aging doesn't follow a single template: while metabolic and cardiovascular strain are often correlated, early kidney decline frequently appears independently. Moreover, the resulting CKM health age gap aligned closely with both objective clinical scores (modified Life's Essential 8 r = −0.58; metabolic syndrome severity r = 0.65) and how healthy participants felt day to day.

Population-level heterogeneity across kidney, metabolic, and cardiovascular systems (teal = healthier than reference; brown = subclinical strain), showing why personalized multi-organ profiling matters.

Looking ahead

Together, these studies show how consumer wearables and machine learning can help shift personal health from looking in the rearview mirror to navigating the road ahead. While our evaluations were conducted offline using retrospective research cohorts, and these models are investigational research prototypes rather than clinical diagnostic tools, they lay the foundation for future prospective trials testing how interactive "what-if" coaching can help people build lasting habits and improve their long-term health.

Acknowledgements

The research described here is joint work across Google Research and partnering teams. Contributors include Zeinab Esmaeilpour, Simon A. Lee, Menglian Zhou, Marius Guerard, Sohrab Sidhu, Alexandru Solot, Hamid Palangi, Pramod Rudrapatna, Ming-Zher Poh, Max A. Xu, Daniel McDuff, Dimitrios Antos, Yuzhe Yang, Jeffrey N. Our world has a fascinating wealth of languages, and for over two decades, Google has been building language technologies that cover as many languages as possible. In 2006, we started a small experiment with Google Translate, supporting just two languages (English and Arabic) at the time. Fast forward to today: nearly 250 languages are supported, with around a trillion words translated every month. Hypertension (i.e., high blood pressure), often called the "silent killer”, affects over one billion people globally, yet more than half of adults with the condition are unaware they have it. Because it rarely presents with obvious symptoms, high blood pressure (BP) is typically discovered only through incidental screening. This gap in awareness is particularly severe among younger adults aged 18 to 44, where missing diagnoses can delay life-saving early interventions and significantly increase the long-term risk of adverse cardiovascular events like stroke or heart failure.

Office BP measurement serves as the primary initial screening gateway for detecting hypertension. In recent years, cuffless wearable devices have emerged as a potential tool to complement episodic office care. However, existing commercial solutions usually require regular calibration using a traditional arm cuff. This means they only track relative changes from a baseline cuff reading rather than identifying absolute hypertensive states, limiting their utility as independent screening tools.

In a new study published in Nature, we present a multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) system capable of passively detecting signs of hypertension using a consumer smartwatch, without requiring any cuff calibration. Dubbed AI-PPG-ACC-HTN, we validated this system against the clinical gold standard of 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM), and it achieves accuracy levels comparable to traditional cuff-based diagnostic workflows for both initial and confirmatory screening. These research findings helped inform the blood pressure trends Health Guardian feature in the Google Health app.

How it works

Instead of attempting to estimate exact, point-in-time systolic and diastolic blood pressure values, which are highly susceptible to transient environmental noise, our system reframes the problem. It focuses on identifying an individual’s underlying, persistent hypertensive state by aggregating passive physiological signatures over multiple days.

The system leverages data from two sensors already active on modern smartwatches:

  • Photoplethysmography (PPG): An optical sensor that tracks changes in blood volume at the wrist by measuring reflected light that captures pulse wave contours.
  • Accelerometry (ACC): A motion sensor that identifies periods of stillness and captures the ballistocardiogram (BCG), the subtle physical vibrations of the wrist caused by the mechanical ejection of blood from the heart into the aorta.

The AI system uses photoplethysmography (PPG) and accelerometer (ACC) signals recorded using a consumer smartwatch to create waveform embeddings. The waveform embeddings are aggregated over time (days) into a person-level embedding, which, along with a user’s height, are used to predict their blood pressure status.

To build this system, we used a two-stage machine learning approach:

Stage 1: Self-supervised pre-training (the waveform encoder)

We trained a 1-D deep convolutional neural network using self-supervised contrastive learning. By analyzing a large, unlabeled dataset of 492,347 hours of sensor data from 2,109 consenting participants, the model learned to map overlapping 15-second PPG and ACC waveforms from the same individual close together in a latent space. This allowed the model to discover complex, physiologically rich features of vascular and mechanical cardiac function without requiring manual feature engineering or medical labels.

Stage 2. Person-level aggregation & classification

For each user, these 15-second feature blocks (embeddings) are mean-aggregated across multiple days of wear to wash out ephemeral noise like sudden movements or temperature changes. Finally, the individual's aggregated embedding is combined with their height (which serves as a reliable proxy for arterial path length) and fed into a regularized logistic regression classifier to calculate a continuous hypertension probability score.

Rigorous validation against the clinical gold standard

To evaluate our system, we conducted a prospective, multi-center clinical study across five US sites involving 196 consenting diverse participants who were free from known cardiovascular disease and not taking blood pressure medications.

Importantly, we benchmarked the smartwatch's performance against 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM), the clinical gold standard for hypertension diagnosis. We evaluated the smartwatch system across two clinical use case scenarios: initial screening and confirmatory testing.

Scenario 1: Initial screening

The smartwatch achieved a moderate sensitivity of 65.8% and a high specificity of 90.0%, resulting in a high positive predictive value (PPV) of 80.6%. In comparison, initial office-based screenings showed a sensitivity of 55.3% and a moderate PPV of 77.8% when benchmarked against the gold standard.

Scenario 2: Confirmatory testing

For individuals who initially screen positive for high blood pressure in a clinic, current guidelines recommend confirmatory out-of-office tracking. We looked at the subset of participants (N=48) who had elevated initial office BP to see how well the smartwatch could confirm sustained hypertension.

Our multimodal system achieved a moderate sensitivity of 78.4%, a high specificity of 90.9% and a high PPV of 96.7%. In comparison, the performance of return office BP measurements showed lower point estimates of sensitivity (67.6%), specificity (63.6%), and PPV (86.2%). Furthermore, the smartwatch approach proved competitive with multi-day home monitoring, which yielded a sensitivity of 89.2%, specificity of 81.8%, and a PPV of 94.3%.

Taken together, the results show that our system can detect hypertension with accuracy levels comparable to traditional cuffed BP devices in the existing clinical framework.

Model interpretability

To gain an understanding of what the AI model may be paying attention to, we visualized the average pulse waveforms from users with the highest and lowest predicted probabilities of hypertension.

We observed the following visual differences:

  • Reduced pulse width: Waveforms linked to a higher risk of hypertension exhibited a slightly narrower pulse width (figure below, top left panel), indicating a smaller change in blood volume, and may suggest stiffer arteries that are less able to expand.
  • Pulse wave reflection: Higher AI risk scores correlated with a slower systolic upstroke (the initial surge of blood) (figure below, highlighted yellow circle in middle panel) and a lower d/a ratio (figure below, highlighted yellow circle in right panel). This specific metric compares the initial forward-traveling pulse wave to the reflected wave bouncing back from the body's vascular network.
  • Mechanical heart vibrations: The smartwatch accelerometer successfully captured the ballistocardiogram (BCG) signal. In users with higher predicted hypertension, we observed distinct physical modulations in these micro-vibrations, specifically deeper "K waves" and wider "IJK complexes" (figure below, highlighted yellow circle in bottom left panel).

Mean pulse waveforms (top left panel), corresponding accelerometer waveforms showing the ballistocardiogram (BCG, bottom left panel), first (middle panel) and second derivatives (right panel) of pulse waveforms from four of the most extreme quintiles of AI-PPG-ACC-HTN scores. Key fiducial points are indicated including the pulse onset (ons), peak (sys), dicrotic notch (dic), diastolic peak (dia) in the PPG waveform, H, I, J, K, L, M, N waves in the BCG waveform, and a, b, c, d, e waves in the second derivative of the PPG waveform.

Outlook

Smartwatch-based hypertension screening is not intended to replace standard clinical arm cuffs or provide a definitive standalone medical diagnosis. Instead, this research points to the potential for a highly scalable, passive tool for opportunistic screening. This work represents early feasibility research and methodologies described here are purely exploratory and are not indicative of any existing or upcoming commercial product feature or device capability. By gently prompting at-risk individuals to step into a clinic for formal assessment, this technology holds the potential to significantly close the global awareness gap and catch hypertension before it causes permanent cardiovascular damage.

Acknowledgements

This research was a collaborative effort between Google Research, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, and Harvard Medical School. We thank our paper co-authors Lawrence Cai, Jiang Wu, Mingwu Gao, Bhavna Daryani, Jonathan Wang, Utkarsh Khanna, Ho Ko, Anupam Pathak, Mark Malhotra, Shwetak Patel, Jacqueline B. Shreibati, Stephen P. Juraschek, Pramod Rudrapatna, and Matthew Thompson. We thank key contributors including: Jennifer Block, Anu Gabbita, Sushalini Sunku, Keerthana Natarajan, Alexandros Pantelopoulos, Tuan Phan, Tracy Giest, and Florence Thng.

Machine learning models learn to recognize the world around us from examples labeled by humans. Underlying this process is an assumption that the person doing the labeling has a clear and stable definition of the category in mind before they begin. This assumption holds well when training a model on objective categories, like a stop sign or a golden retriever, where boundaries are clear and universally recognized. In practice, however, real-world applications often require vision systems to navigate the subjective "gray areas" of human experience. For example, consider training a vision classifier to identify "healthy food", curate "inspiring artwork”, or assist in content moderation. In such domains, category boundaries may not be universal or static, since they can shift with cultural context, personal philosophies, or evolving operational policies. Furthermore, people rarely start with a complete specification for subjective concepts, even in their own minds. Instead, they begin with an intuitive idea of a concept and only discover the concept’s true boundaries, exceptions, and nuances as they encounter real-world examples. Traditional training workflows don’t account for this concept evolution, forcing users to provide rigid labels to an AI system even when their own mental model is still shifting.

To bridge this gap, we introduce Agile Deliberation, a framework that treats the creation of subjective AI classifiers as an iterative conversation. Rather than requiring humans to act as static data labelers, Agile Deliberation turns the AI system into a collaborative partner that helps users "deliberate" and sharpen their own definitions. By resolving human ambiguity first, the framework systematically builds more effective, robust, and aligned AI systems. To support the wider research community, we have also open-sourced the underlying code and algorithms on GitHub.

A key differentiator of this work is its focus on the live user experience. Because standard, static AI benchmarks can’t capture subjective concepts, we bypassed simulated testing and evaluated Agile Deliberation across 18 live, 1.5-hour sessions with human participants. This allowed us to directly observe and measure how a person's intent dynamically evolves when paired with an intelligent system. We found that Agile Deliberation drastically reduced user fatigue and anxiety by replacing manual prompt engineering with direct feedback on borderline images, which resulted in more consistent, higher-performing AI models that outperform standard baselines.

How it works: The two stages of deliberation

Agile Deliberation splits the complex task of defining a subjective concept into two structured stages: concept scoping and concept iteration. Together, these two phases transform a fuzzy idea into a highly precise instructional blueprint for an AI model.

The Agile Deliberation workflow. The framework decomposes a broad target concept into in-scope (i.e., positive examples that the classifier should recognize and flag as matching the user's intent) and out-of-scope (i.e., explicit negative boundaries or "false alarms" that the user wants the classifier not to flag) definitions, retrieves borderline images to expose edge cases, and guides human feedback into an automatic prompt refinement loop to generate ready-to-use image classifiers.

Stage 1: Concept scoping

When confronted with a broad topic like "Healthy Food," human intuition naturally struggles to list every rule upfront. In the concept scoping stage, the system guides the user to break down their overarching concept into a structured hierarchy of sub-concepts and explicit exclusions.

For instance, instead of just using a single broad label, a user might decompose "Healthy Food" into positive sub-categories like "Salads," "Grain Bowls," and "Lean Proteins." Simultaneously, they might define explicit exclusions, such as "Processed Foods" or "Raw, Unprepared Ingredients." This creates an initial structured baseline that grounds the model's understanding.

Stage 2: Concept iteration

With the initial structure established, the framework moves from static planning to active testing. Traditional machine learning assumes the human annotator is an "oracle" with a complete set of fully defined rules already in mind. Agile Deliberation upends this premise, focusing instead on collaborative refinement.

This stage draws inspiration from active learning, a method traditionally used to retrieve informative data points to maximize a machine's training efficiency. However, instead of selecting examples purely to minimize machine uncertainty as in active learning, Agile Deliberation uses vision-language models (VLMs) to actively mine and surface semantically borderline images that challenge the current text-based definitions.

For instance, the system might present an image of a fruit smoothie to challenge a "healthy diet" concept, forcing the user to decide: Is this a healthy beverage because it contains raw fruit, or is it an excluded processed food due to high sugar content?

Confronting these ambiguous edge cases drives users to reflect on their own hidden assumptions, clarify their true intent, and update the policy rules accordingly. This human feedback is then routed directly into an automatic prompt optimization loop, ensuring the VLM's classification boundaries shift in tandem with the user’s refined definitions.

Experiments

Evaluating subjective visual classifiers presents a fundamental challenge: there is no static, objective ground truth to measure performance against and therefore, offline evaluation on pre-labeled datasets can’t measure how well the framework adapts as a person's mental model of a concept shifts during the deliberation process.

To capture this dynamic, we built a functional prototype and evaluated it through a live user study. We conducted 18 live user sessions, each lasting 1.5 hours, where participants interacted with our system and alternative baselines in a randomized order to prevent learning bias.

We chose two complex, highly subjective domains to test the limits of these systems:

  • Healthy Food: A domain where personal health philosophies, dietary restrictions, and cultural backgrounds can produce highly diverse, subjective viewpoints.
  • Pay-to-Play: A real-world content moderation challenge that requires capturing expert-level nuance and specific context. This involves identifying clickbait images in online entertainment or gaming that promise misleading financial or digital rewards.

We evaluated Agile Deliberation against three common distinct paradigms:

  1. Zero-shot classifiers: The standard "one-and-done" approach. Users write an initial prompt, but have no way to see edge cases or adapt when the model misinterprets the boundary.
  2. Modeling collaborator: An automated, top-down approach where an AI agent tries to decompose the concept on its own. While it generates criteria automatically, it removes the user from the loop, leaving no way to guide or correct its logic.
  3. Manual deliberation: The tedious, brute-force status quo process, where users examine data in spreadsheets, guess search queries to find anomalies, and rewrite raw prompts by hand.

Results

The live user sessions revealed that Agile Deliberation yields higher-performing classifier models, while substantially improving the user experience.

Improving consistency and performance

We found that study participants who went through the structured deliberation process demonstrated significantly higher labeling consistency over time. By resolving boundary ambiguities early on, they built classifiers that substantially outperformed all standard baselines. These performance gains were most dramatic on the most challenging subjective images — the exact areas where traditional classifiers typically fail because they rely on default, generic AI assumptions rather than the user's explicit, nuanced intent.

Eliminating blind spots

Expert participants reported that the system acted as an effective diagnostic tool. By intentionally serving up confusing, borderline images, the AI system helped them uncover "blind spots" in their initial definitions — uncovering scenarios they hadn't anticipated until presented with ambiguous real-world examples.

Classifier performance gains across tasks. Across both "Pay-to-Play" and "Healthy Food" evaluation groups, the Agile Deliberation framework yields consistent performance gains over zero-shot baselines, whereas manual deliberation methods often fail to improve or even degrade classifier accuracy.

Alleviating cognitive fatigue

A key finding of our live study was the cognitive toll of manual prompt engineering. Our study showed that users experienced pronounced cognitive fatigue when trying to predict search terms that might uncover edge cases during manual concept deliberation. Furthermore, they reported experiencing persistent anxiety that manually tweaking a text prompt to fix one mistake might unintentionally degrade performance for other parts of the classifier they had already fixed.

User experience and cognitive load metrics. Compared to traditional manual prompt engineering, participants using Agile Deliberation reported statistically significant reductions in required effort and stress, alongside lower mental demand and higher perceived success and ease of use.

Agile Deliberation addresses this friction by handling the heavy computational lifting. Users don't need to be prompt engineers; they simply look at a curated gallery of borderline images and provide natural feedback. In such domains, category boundaries may not be universal or static, since they can shift with cultural context, personal philosophies, or evolving operational policies. Furthermore, people rarely start with a complete specification for subjective concepts, even in their own minds. Instead, they begin with an intuitive idea of a concept and only discover the concept’s true boundaries, exceptions, and nuances as they encounter real-world examples. Traditional training workflows don’t account for this concept evolution, forcing users to provide rigid labels to an AI system even when their own mental model is still shifting.
To bridge this gap, we introduce Agile Deliberation, a framework that treats the creation of subjective AI classifiers as an iterative conversation. Rather than requiring humans to act as static data labelers, Agile Deliberation turns the AI system into a collaborative partner that helps users "deliberate" and sharpen their own definitions. By resolving human ambiguity first, the framework systematically builds more effective, robust, and aligned AI systems. To support the wider research community, we have also open-sourced the underlying code and algorithms on GitHub.
A key differentiator of this work is its focus on the live user experience. Because standard, static AI benchmarks can’t capture subjective concepts, we bypassed simulated testing and evaluated Agile Deliberation across 18 live, 1.5-hour sessions with human participants. items.content:
Modern LLMs achieve impressive performance via pre-training and in-context learning (ICL). However, once deployed, they remain largely static, operating with a fixed knowledge cutoff date that leaves them unable to acquire long-term capabilities or adapt to new information.

While updating models with new data seems like the obvious solution, continual parameter updates often trigger catastrophic forgetting, a fundamental issue where learning new tasks severely degrades performance on previously learned ones. Alternatively, relying strictly on ICL limits knowledge retention to the immediate context window: once the context session ends, the acquired short-term information is forgotten.

Inspired by how the human brain processes and stabilizes memory during rest, we introduce a sleep framework in continual learning: a learning paradigm that equips large language models (LLMs) with a continuous periodic lifecycle, enabling them to continually learn, consolidate fragile short-term context into stable long-term parameters. With this framework, we demonstrate that alternating between active interaction and offline memory consolidation allows LLMs to continuously acquire new facts, retain long-context knowledge up to 10M tokens, and improve complex reasoning.

Rethinking machine learning: Active (wake) vs. sleep phases

Traditional machine learning relies on a strict separation between training and inference. In a continual learning framework, this distinction becomes artificial; an intelligent agent must constantly learn, adapt, and process information.

Under the sleep paradigm, an LLM operates across two primary states:

  1. Active (wake) phase: The model actively receives, processes, and interacts with inputs, storing temporary information in fast, short-term memory components.
  2. Sleep phase: The model pauses processing new inputs and redirects its internal computations toward memory consolidation and self-improvement.

While terms like "sleep," "dreaming," and "self-improvement" borrow from neuroscience, our framework operates entirely within a fixed model architecture and human-defined training rules. During the offline sleep phase, the model unlocks pre-allocated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) memory blocks and updates its numerical weights using self-generated practice examples. This automated post-training cycle helps a deployed model absorb new facts and sharpen its reasoning accuracy while keeping its core codebase and design unchanged.

Key components of the sleep process

The sleep paradigm addresses catastrophic forgetting and continuous adaptation through two stages: memory consolidation and dreaming.

1. Memory consolidation

In the human brain, non-rapid eye movement (NREM) slow-wave sleep consolidates fragile memories into long-term structures via abstraction and distillation. Our proposed sleep framework mirrors this natural phenomenon through two key technical mechanisms:

  • Parameter expansion & continuum memory hierarchy: To prevent catastrophic forgetting, the model dynamically scales its capacity during sleep. Using a Mixture of Experts (MoE) and Hope architecture , newly unlocked, low-rank experts are integrated into stable, lower-frequency memory blocks to store incoming knowledge without disrupting older parameters.
  • Knowledge seeding (upward distillation): Fragile short-term memories stored in high-frequency layers (e.g., in-context memory) are transferred into the newly expanded long-term parameters. This is achieved through Generalized Knowledge Distillation (GKD) combined with reinforcement learning (RL)-based imitation learning:
    • On-policy distillation: The expanded student model learns token-specific feedback from teacher distributions generated on self-sampled sequences.
    • Learning to imitate (LTI): The student model is rewarded based on semantic and absolute similarity (Levenshtein distance) when completing prefixes of teacher-generated text.
  • Synaptic pruning: Once the memory consolidation into lower-frequency modules is complete, the high-frequency temporary parameters are reset, freeing up capacity for future active sessions.

Overview of our sleep framework: Input streams from the active phase are stored in short-term memory before entering the sleep cycle, which bifurcates into Consolidation (transferring fragile short-term tokens into expanded long-term parametric memory using low-rank structures and MoE) and Dreaming (autonomous self-improvement via synthetic routing with random experts and RL refinement).

2. Dreaming for self-improvement

During REM sleep, the human brain actively simulates scenarios, consolidates emotional/semantic connections, and explores novel neural pathways. Mirroring this, during the “dreaming stage”, the sleep framework implements an autonomous self-improvement loop:

  • Random expert selection: During synthetic data generation, the MoE router randomly activates non-standard experts. This forces the model to mix disparate domains of knowledge and uncover latent patterns.
  • Curated rehearsal: The model generates synthetic training samples ("dreams") and filters them using gradient-based data selection to prioritize samples with the highest potential to boost overall model capability.
  • RL refinement: The model performs supervised fine-tuning on top-rated dream samples and evaluates whether the generation improves performance on downstream tasks.

Theoretical foundations

Beyond the empirical results, our sleep paradigm is grounded in a theory that clarifies why its two stages (memory consolidation and dreaming) can support continual learning without simply trading new knowledge for old capabilities.

For memory consolidation, the analysis shows that knowledge seeding can be understood as a structured, low-rank compression problem. The model is not asked to copy every detail of its short-term traces into its parameters. Instead, it identifies a compact set of directions that best preserve both the model’s own on-policy behavior and the semantic qualities rewarded by the learning objective.

This perspective explains the complementary roles of the two signals: on-policy distillation aligns consolidation with the trajectories the model will actually produce at inference time, reducing the mismatch that can arise when training only on teacher-generated distributions; meanwhile, the semantic reward changes what is worth retaining, prioritizing directions that preserve meaning and task-relevant behavior rather than merely matching token probabilities. Parameter expansion then provides the capacity needed to write these selected memories without overwriting previously consolidated knowledge.

For dreaming, the theory characterizes random expert activation and reward-based sample selection as mechanisms for improving the geometry of learning. Injecting different MoEs broadens the set of gradient directions explored during synthetic generation, exposing the model to a richer collection of updates than those induced by its ordinary wake-time data alone. Gradient-based filtering then emphasizes the synthetic experiences that carry the most useful learning signal, strengthening informative directions while preserving the structure of the underlying gradient space.

Together, these steps yield a more balanced optimization landscape: learning is less dominated by a small number of directions, gradients are better conditioned, and the model can make more stable progress when refining its capabilities. In this view, dreaming is not simply self-generated data augmentation; it is a deliberate process for diversifying, selecting, and consolidating the updates through which the model improves itself.

Comparative performance of our sleep framework against baseline approaches (such as in-context learning and supervised fine-tuning) across major evaluation axes, including Class-Incremental Learning, continual translation, long-context scaling up to 10M tokens, factual knowledge incorporation, and mathematical reasoning.

For continual translation, in unseen languages, such as Manchu and Kalamang, the sleep framework maintained a near-zero performance drop in multi-stage evaluations, whereas standard baselines like ICL, Cartridges, and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) suffered severe catastrophic forgetting during sequential learning.

In long-context understanding on the BABILong benchmark, our sleep method demonstrated near-perfect scaling up to 10M tokens, outperforming strong baselines like GPT-4, and Titans by using sleep-time consolidation to compress long-context information directly into parametric memory.

For factual knowledge incorporation evaluated on SQuAD and continued pre-training (CPT), our sleep method achieved 48.9% on single-task and 46.2% on CPT evaluations, outperforming baseline methods including the base model, SFT, and Self-Adapting Language Models (SEAL) by successfully integrating new factual information without degrading existing model representations.

Finally, on mathematical reasoning benchmarks including AIME 24/25 and HMMT 25, sleep-enhanced base-model achieved accuracy scores of 79.2%, 69.0%, and 46.1%, respectively. This outperformed baselines like SFT, group relative policy optimization (GRPO), and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), showing that pairing memory consolidation with imitation learning drives superior reasoning performance.

Conclusion

Our sleep paradigm provides a path toward autonomous, continually learning AI systems. By moving beyond static pre-training and fragile context windows, alternating between active learning and offline rest empowers LLMs to retain short-term memories, abstract new skills into long-term parameter structures, and continuously self-improve without catastrophic forgetting.

Acknowledgements

This research was conducted by Ali Behrouz (Google and Cornell University), Farnoosh Hashemi (Cornell University), Adel Javanmard (Google and University of Southern California), and Vahab Mirrokni. We thank Yuan Deng and Corinna Cortes for reviewing the work and their valuable suggestions. We also thank Mark Simborg, Kimberly Schwede, and Tim Herrmann for their help in crafting this blog post.

Getting access to timely healthcare often comes down to an accident of geography: where you live, what resources your local clinic possesses, and whether a specialist is within reach.

Nowhere is this disparity more acute than in the fight against tuberculosis (TB). Despite being preventable and curable, TB claims more than 1.23 million lives annually. A primary bottleneck is radiology: For those in high-burden settings, from people who live in remote rural areas to miners working deep underground, radiologists are scarce, and imaging infrastructure is often days away. As a result, millions of active cases go undetected, perpetuating transmission.

Over the past several years, our team across Google Research and Google for Health has worked to change that trajectory: moving from an AI-based tool that builds on our existing work in medical imaging to identify people with presumptive TB for follow-up testing to prospective clinical trials, regulatory clearance with local partners, and ultimately open foundation models like MedGemma that empower public health systems worldwide. This week at IDWeek 2026 in Washington, D.C., we are sharing how we’re bringing health AI research to reality, and how foundational models can democratize TB screening at global scale.

Proving AI-based tools can read chest radiographs

Our work began with a fundamental question: Can AI-based tools interpret chest radiographs (CXRs) with the accuracy of an expert radiologist for TB screening?

Chest radiography is the frontline imaging modality for pulmonary screening, but detecting subtle signs of TB like apical infiltrates (fluid in the top portion of the lung) and cavitary lesions (tissue damage) requires specialized expertise that is rarely available in rural clinics. In 2019, we published a benchmark in Radiology, demonstrating that deep learning algorithms could detect active pulmonary TB at performance levels matching experienced radiologists.

Real-world utility, however, demands independent verification. In August 2021, the Stop TB Partnership evaluated automated computer-aided detection (CAD) software across diverse patient cohorts in The Lancet Digital Health, ranking our model among the top-performing TB screening algorithms globally. That year, WHO also recommended CAD for TB screening and triage. In September 2024, in NEJM AI, we detailed a prospective, multi-site validation demonstrating that AI-assisted screening maintains high sensitivity (minimizing missed cases) across diverse patient populations, while also reliably detecting other incidental pulmonary and cardiac abnormalities.

Navigating the translation gap

In medical AI, publishing a paper is only the beginning. Between an algorithmic model and a trusted bedside tool lies the "translation gap": making software reliable across varied X-ray machines and offline settings, integrating it into clinical workflows, and meeting medical device regulations.

With this in mind, we partnered with Nexus AI, a Pretoria-based medical technology company, and they translated our chest X-ray algorithms into a certified clinical diagnostic tool. Navigating the regulatory landscape required extensive audits:

  • CE MDR class IIb certification: Under the European Union’s Medical Device Regulation (EU MDR 2017/745), Nexus AI achieved Class IIb certification — a rigorous designation that verifies the tool is safe for real-world patient care based on prospective clinical evaluations.
  • Quality standards: Nexus AI obtained certified compliance with ISO 13485 for medical device quality management.
  • Global access: Nexus AI signed an agreement with FIND to pursue the World Health Organization Pre-qualification (WHO PQ), which is essential for international procurement through global agencies, alongside an ongoing pathway toward the U.S. FDA clearance.

The Nexus AI device screens chest X-rays for lung diseases like TB in as little as 45 seconds.

Frontline impact: Reaching patients where they are

Today, Nexus Intelligence is actively deploying this technology where diagnostic access is most urgently needed.

Across six countries — South Africa, Sierra Leone, and Côte d'Ivoire, with expansions underway in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Zambia, and Cameroon — Nexus AI’s tool operates in approximately 40 healthcare facilities. To date, over 90 clinicians have evaluated more than 25,000 chest radiographs, reducing turnaround times from weeks to under 45 seconds, accelerating rapid triage while empowering healthcare professionals to make final clinical decisions.

Our collaboration commits to health equity: Nexus AI has delivered more than 3,000 free screenings to under-resourced public clinics, progressing toward a goal of 10,000 sponsored screenings annually.

Screening at the extremes: The Mponeng Gold Mine

Perhaps no deployment better illustrates meeting patients where they are than the work done at the Mponeng Gold Mine in South Africa, one of the deepest mines in the world. Deep-shaft miners face chronic silica dust exposure and an elevated risk of pulmonary disease. In partnership with the Stop TB Partnership, Harmony Gold Mine, and the South African Department of Health, Nexus AI deployed ultra-portable digital X-ray kits and offline AI four kilometers underground. Miners are screened on-site within seconds, and those flagged with presumptive TB can be immediately referred for confirmatory molecular testing. Screening, triage and confirmatory testing can now happen in a single visit, compressing a pathway that often takes weeks.

From point solution to open foundations: HAI-DEF and MedGemma

A custom solution with a single partner cannot address the global TB burden alone. To scale impact, we shifted from isolated deployments to building open, adaptable foundations that allow developers and health ministries to create solutions tailored to local needs.

Through the Health AI Developer Foundations (HAI-DEF), we open-sourced our chest X-ray embeddings and MedSigLIP, a lightweight vision-language model trained to align medical images, such as chest X-rays, with the clinical language used to describe them. Because MedSigLIP understands both images and text, developers can use it to classify or search images with plain-language labels, or fine-tune it for a specific task with only a small set of local examples. This lets local teams build specialized models on modest regional datasets and reach strong performance without massive compute resources.

Building on this, we released MedGemma, a family of open-weight multimodal models (4B and 27B parameter configurations). MedGemma advances from basic classification to multimodal clinical reasoning: it synthesizes radiographic findings with clinical history, answers clinician queries in natural language, and runs locally on-device without internet access. Since its launch, MedGemma has seen more than 10 million downloads worldwide.

Nexus AI’s application analyzes a chest X-ray integrating models, which highlights findings that are not consistent with normal lung fields, including findings suggestive of tuberculosis, and when further investigation is required (FIR).

Sovereign scale: Supporting Indonesia’s national TB initiative

Open models help enable public health systems to build sovereign solutions that protect patient privacy. In Southeast Asia, the Ministry of Health of Indonesia is addressing the world's second-highest TB burden with an ambitious goal: screening 50 million citizens annually to eradicate the disease.

Reviewing 50 million X-rays manually is infeasible, and proprietary cloud software poses data residency challenges. Instead, the Ministry is fine-tuning MedGemma and MedSigLIP on domestic chest radiographs. Because the models run on local infrastructure, patient data remains within national borders, giving health leaders full sovereignty over clinical deployment.

Complementary screening: Bioacoustics with HeAR

Recognizing that imaging equipment cannot reach every remote health post, Google Research also developed Health Acoustic Representations (HeAR). Trained on over 300 million audio segments, HeAR enables non-invasive acoustic screening from cough sounds recorded on a standard smartphone microphone.

HeAR is being utilized through collaborative research across sub-Saharan Africa with CIDRZ (Zambia), the Aurum Institute (Ghana, supported by a $250,000 Google.org grant), and HELINA’s $1.5 million regional collaborative. Together, acoustic triage (HeAR), mobile X-ray screening (HAI-DEF), and multimodal clinical reasoning (MedGemma) offer communities an integrated diagnostic cascade of tools for underserved populations.

Looking ahead

The journey from a laboratory algorithm to a CE-certified tool used in clinics across six countries has shown us what it takes to turn research into real-world impact: rigorous science, open developer platforms, and dedicated local partnerships. Because our partners know their communities best, they are now taking this work further. Nexus AI is expanding to new countries, Indonesia is integrating TB screening into its national program, and CIDRZ, the Aurum Institute and HELINA are building the clinical evidence for cough-based triage. Our role is to help equip them with open models, foundational research and ongoing support, so that more people with TB are diagnosed and treated sooner.

At IDWeek 2026, we look forward to connecting with the infectious disease and public health communities as we work together to expand equitable care.

Acknowledgements

We thank our collaborators at Nexus AI, Stop TB Partnership, UNOPS, CIDRZ, Aurum Institute, HELINA, Harmony Gold Mine, the South African Department of Health, and the Indonesian Ministry of Health for their clinical leadership and dedication to global health equity.

The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that more than 250,000 preventable deaths occur worldwide each year due to pregnancy-related complications. While prenatal ultrasound can improve outcomes and reduce fetal and maternal mortality, two-thirds of people globally lack access to diagnostic medical imaging like ultrasound. Current methods that support maternal health rely heavily on specialized clinical training, leaving millions in low-resource settings without access to a single ultrasound during their entire pregnancy.

We saw an opportunity to conduct research towards addressing this real-world need, by developing machine learning systems that interpret "blind sweep" ultrasounds. This way of scanning allows frontline healthcare workers without specialized sonography training to perform scans by simply gliding low-cost, portable ultrasound probes across the abdomen in a standardized pattern.
