Blind sweep sequence protocol diagram in order of their appearance in the data collection protocol.

Because many regions face critical shortages of experts, and traditional sonographer training is both expensive and requires a multi-year commitment, enabling these health workers to perform assessments with minimal training has the potential to significantly expand prenatal screening coverage.

Combining the minimal training requirement with AI interpretations could ultimately mean a successfully developed tool that has the potential to increase availability of ultrasound-based pregnancy assessment, and thereby improve access to higher quality maternal health.

In “Generalization of AI-Based Gestational Age Assessment Using Blind Sweep Ultrasonography”, published in JAMA Network Open, we evaluated how effectively an AI model for gestational age assessment (how far along the pregnancy is) generalizes across diverse clinical settings and hardware. While our previous research validated the model's performance on unseen patients from the same retrospective cohort it learned from, this new prospective study shows how the AI system performs reliably running live on mobile devices in real clinics, with only novice operators and unfamiliar ultrasound equipment, and minimal fine-tuning.

“The gestational age is basically how far along a woman is in pregnancy. All of our screening, a lot of our treatments, a lot of our indications for delivery are all based on this master timeline that you get from the gestational age.”

- Nichole Young-Lin, OB-GYN Physician

Evaluating performance across diverse clinical settings

For a medical AI system to safely scale globally, it must demonstrate generalizability — maintaining accurate diagnostic performance when introduced to new clinical settings with different patient populations, clinical workflows, and ultrasound hardware variations than those on which the model was trained.

In this study, our original AI model was minimally tuned on only one of our target populations, and then prospectively tested across both target environments:

  • Northwestern Medicine: An urban, high-resource academic medical center in Chicago, IL, United States.
  • Jacaranda Health: An urban community clinic network in Nairobi, Kenya.

Originally trained on ultrasound data collected in North Carolina and Zambia using a set of Sonosite, GE, and Butterfly Networks commercial ultrasound probes, the research AI system was paired with Clarius C3, a commercial handheld transabdominal probe. All of these sites differed in various care dimensions, including when women first come in for prenatal care, how many routine ultrasounds they receive, and how gestational age is usually dated.

To evaluate efficient system tuning, the study leveraged a small pilot dataset of 120 participants from Chicago — approximately 6% of the original training set—to adapt the model to new probe hardware and extend the gestational age prediction range beyond 36 weeks. To understand generalizability, no data from the Nairobi site was used for fine-tuning, maintaining the Kenyan clinical validation as a strictly independent, external test. To evaluate comprehensive utility, the study also included multiple gestation pregnancies, which could present tracking and measurement challenges for both human operators and automated systems.

Our blind sweep model, trained on 1,968 participants (North Carolina, US, and Zambia) was fine-tuned on scans from 120 participants from Chicago, Illinois. It was then tested prospectively in Chicago (n=192) and Nairobi (n=193), with no fine-tuning on Nairobi data. The model was non-inferior to expert sonographers at determining gestational age, in both settings, with a combined mean absolute error of 4.18 vs. 4.48 days.

Key findings: Matching the expert standard

We compared the AI system’s ability to estimate fetal age from blind sweep ultrasounds to formula-based estimation from the clinically standard expert approach. This expert approach relies on an expert sonographer locating multiple specific cross-sections of the fetus(es) to take precise biometry measurements, a difficult-to-scale task that requires years of training and is highly operator-dependent.

Evaluating a primary cohort of 385 participants between 16 and 36 weeks of pregnancy, the diagnostic study demonstrated strong AI system results:

  • Clinically non-inferior accuracy: Across both cohorts, the AI model achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 4.18 days in estimating gestational age, successfully demonstrating non-inferiority to the standard clinical procedure performed by expert sonographers, which had an MAE of 4.48 days.
  • Cross-setting generalization: In Chicago, the adapted model achieved an MAE of 4.10 days. In Nairobi, with zero local optimization, the model achieved a comparable MAE of 4.27 days.

The AI system's gestational age error (MAE 4.18 days) was non-inferior to expert sonographer biometry (4.48 days), and stayed consistent from Chicago (4.10 days) to Nairobi (4.27 days), where the model had no local fine-tuning.

Beyond accuracy, exploratory metrics showed that the research AI system was resilient in complex scenarios. For instance, in cases of fetal weight extremes (above the 90th percentile), the model outperformed traditional biometry formulas, demonstrating robustness against variations in fetal size.

Lessons learned during prospective deployment

In addition to highlighting an immense opportunity to expand ultrasound access through AI, the prospective multi-center study allowed us to actively observe and optimize how AI behaves in live clinical environments. By deploying our system directly into everyday clinical workflows, we gained practical insights that help us design for real world use. For example, we observed the importance of swappable batteries over plug-in docking stations for keeping devices charged between consecutive patients.

These studies also demonstrated how deploying AI systems like this will also require building deep trust with both clinicians and patients. One important way to ultimately achieve this would be by building clear safeguards into the app, like model confidence estimates produced by our model to reject poor-quality sweeps and convey model uncertainty to the clinician user.

Looking ahead: Expanding access to care with AI

These study findings indicate that AI-based systems can analyze standardized “blind sweeps” images acquired by operators without specialized sonography training. The AI estimate of fetal age had accuracy comparable to the current standard of care from expert operators and more expensive traditional, cart-based ultrasound machines. Demonstrating technical generalizability across diverse clinical settings, hardware, and changing populations, marks a key step in highlighting their potential to expand access to this critical capability for maternal health.

By empowering minimally trained community health workers to perform reliable ultrasonography assessments, this research demonstrates the potential to expand prenatal coverage for millions in under-resourced areas. Studying the capabilities of this scalable technology lays the groundwork for more resilient, accessible healthcare systems, ensuring that every mother, regardless of location, has the chance for a healthy pregnancy and a safe delivery.

This point-of-care research represents a potential application of our broader vision for expanding healthcare accessibility through AI. The insights gained from this research inform the development of our next-generation, multimodal medical intelligence research. Through our continued work, we strive to provide the development community and scientists with the answers they need to improve clinical care and make it helpful and accessible to all.

Acknowledgements

Thank you to our co-authors across Google Research, Jacaranda Health and Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine: Chace Lee, Justin Krogue, Anneka Wickramanayake, Stacey Caron, Priscah Cheruiyot, Amber Watters, Alicia Martín, Tiya Tiyasirichokchai, Akib Uddin, Yun Liu, Patricia Strachan, Sunny Jansen, Alyssa Santi, Preeti Singh, Catherine Arguelles, Kenneth Hudson, David Melnick, Mahesh Vaidyanathan, Mozziyar Etemadi, Yossi Matias, Avinatan Hassidim, Greg Corrado, Shruthi Prabhakara, Daniel Golden, Ryan G. Gomes, and Shravya Shetty. Thank you to Pi-Chuan Chang and Dale Webster for reviewing this work.

items.content:
Frontier AI systems have the potential to transform biology research and drug discovery by intelligently navigating vast combinatorial search spaces (e.g., a single 100-amino-acid protein spans at least 20100 possible sequences) calling for dynamic multi-candidate exploration. Our long-term research vision is that AI agents will not only ideate and analyze, but also run lab experiments to test their hypotheses, learn from the results, and self-improve to solve complex problems — all driven by human scientific agency.

Realizing this vision requires solving two intertwined challenges: First, frontier models still do not reason reliably about 3-dimensional geometry and physical state — which poses a problem in the automation of the specialized liquid-handling robots that move reagents, track volumes, and execute molecular biology protocols in a wet lab. Second, while agentic hypothesis generation and in-silico design are advancing rapidly, needing repeated cycles of real-world feedback to validate the proposals and navigate vast search spaces, real-world wet-lab experiments have not kept pace, making experimental readouts more of a bottleneck than ever.

In this post we share three research projects highlighting our progress on bridging the gap between in-silico AI exploration and real-world wet-lab experimentation:

  • Enabling AI agents to perform safe, resource efficient experimentation grounded in physical measurements by using the VERID framework.
  • Demonstrating closed-loop agentic scientific discoveries on our prototypes for aptamer and de-novo protein design.

Grounding agents in physical reality

First, we present the VERified Infrastructure for Discovery Laboratories (VERID) framework to bridge the gap between the high-level reasoning of AI agents and the complex, error-prone physical reality of a wet lab. It is a semantic digital twin of the laboratory workcell, i.e., a live, stateful 3D volumetric entity tree that tracks everything from robotic arm geometry to individual well volumes, reagent identities, and pipette tip inventory.

The safety of a command depends on the live physical context as well as the code. An agent can generate syntactically valid code that is physically impossible (e.g., lowering an 8-channel pipette into a narrow trough that is too short), logistically invalid (e.g., aspirating from a depleted well), or scientifically compromised by unmodeled fluidic effects.

Through VERID, an AI agent plans, simulates, and executes liquid-handling protocols on a liquid handling robot, combining synchronized multi-camera views with live state tracking to refine experiments across cycles.

Built on top of the open-source PyLabRobot framework, VERID provides four core capabilities:

  • Live 3D state tracking: Allow agents to check deck layout, well volumes, and available tips before acting.
  • Fast virtual dry runs: Simulate protocols in seconds to catch collisions or empty wells before touching reagents.
  • Hardware safety checks: Block invalid commands before they reach the robot.
  • Synchronized video and action logs: Capture a complete record of every run for research rigor, reproducibility, and debugging.

In our report, we show these capabilities in action through case studies. First, synchronized video and execution traces caught uneven dye stratification caused by dispensing too close to the well floor, allowing the agent to refine its mixing strategy. In the same campaign, the persistent digital twin state allowed the agent to recover mid-run from a plate-reader failure without re-pipetting. Second, when the simulator rejected an 8-channel aspiration that physically wouldn't fit in a narrow trough, the agent replanned on the fly and designed a targeted factorial diagnostic isolating a subtle bias caused by residual tip-wall carryover that replication alone would have missed. Finally, in a closed-loop self-play campaign, an agent iteratively designed and ran robot experiments to reconstruct blinded dye mixtures from overhead camera images, identifying its own optical and fluidic artifacts across runs to improve accuracy more than fivefold.

Reproducible execution and full trace logs — capturing procedural variables like dwell times, evaporation, and plate layout — lay the groundwork for agents to eventually be able to separate biological signals from experimental noise as they explore and refine many candidates in parallel across rounds.

Learning to learn with aptamers

Agents need real experimental readouts to refine their hypotheses as computational models do not capture the full picture of what happens in a wet-lab reaction and cannot replace empirical validation. In “Aptamers as a sandbox for lab-in-the-loop agentic molecular discovery”, we use protein-binding DNA aptamers to prototype the lab in a closed loop with AI agents over 3 design-test-iteration cycles. Aptamer discovery is a type of experiment common in research efforts for clinical biomarker discovery. A complete aptamer design-test-analyze cycle takes just 7–10 days, as DNA can be chemically synthesized in pooled libraries and read out directly by sequencing. In each round, agents design candidate sequences, which are screened against target proteins on magnetic beads to isolate functional binders, and then sequenced to return rich quantitative data for the next cycle.

Agents iteratively design, synthesize, select, and sequence aptamers in a closed loop.

Across three rounds on two protein targets with varying difficulty levels (myoglobin and α-thrombin), AI-driven rational and de novo design raised confirmed on-target hit rates as can be seen in the image below (to 33.5% and 42.1% for myoglobin and α-thrombin, respectively), though each target required identifying and overcoming a different wet-lab failure mode.

On α-thrombin, Round 1 yielded 0% binders because fixed primer overhangs disrupted folding in 48% of sequences; once the agents introduced clamped flanking stems in Round 2 and diversified in Round 3, hit rates climbed to 26.0% and then 42.1% at 98.5% specificity.

On myoglobin, as agents prioritized raw binding affinity in Round 2, they heavily enriched G-quadruplex motifs (63% of designs). While raw pull-down increased, the wet-lab data showed that most of these G-quadruplexes were non-specific "sticky" binders adhering to off-target proteins and bare magnetic beads, causing both target specificity (from 75.0% to 19.1%) and true, bead-corrected hit rate (from 10.2% to 3.7%) to plunge. Recognizing this artifact from the Round 2 readout, the agents autonomously revised their design rules for Round 3, capping promiscuous motifs, subtracting bead binders, and pivoting to non-G4 structural scaffolds to recover specificity (72.4%) and surge ninefold in on-target hit rate (33.5%).

Across three rounds, agents learn from wet-lab readouts to recover target specificity and improve confirmed de novo hit rates on myoglobin (left) and α-thrombin (right).

In the paper, we also examine how agents reason like scientists, analyzing data and suggesting tweaks to wet-lab protocols, but also sometimes think atypically, exploring sequence spaces that structural biologists might not.

Accelerating de novo protein binder design

Closing the loop for proteins is more complex. Unlike aptamers, which are chemically synthesized, proteins must be expressed biologically, so each loop adds cellular or cell-free selection, expression, and folding steps. Together with a larger sequence space, this creates bottlenecks on both the computational and wet-lab sides.

In “Agent-guided epitope excision enables economical de novo binder design”, we applied our workflow to fibroblast activation protein alpha (FAP), a large, challenging receptor overexpressed in solid tumors. In just a few experimental runs, the top designs yielded binders with single-digit nanomolar affinity, a level of tight, drug-like binding typically achieved only after extensive rounds of laboratory optimization.

Surgical epitope excision accelerates structure prediction 8.6x (left), enabling a human–agent hybrid pipeline to nearly double the in-silico hit rate (top right) and discover single-digit nanomolar FAP binders in the wet lab (bottom right).

Computationally, de novo binder design requires generating candidate backbones, designing sequences to fit them, and re-folding the resulting complexes to predict binding. That final re-folding step consumes the vast majority of GPU compute, as it scales quadratically with target length. By surgically excising just the local binding pocket during folding, our pipeline accelerated each cycle more than eightfold without losing structural accuracy. This turns decisions about where to bind and how much surrounding structure to include into tactical levers that LLM agents are well-suited to optimize.

In a head-to-head comparison at equal compute, human–agent collaboration, where a scientist sets the high-level strategy and an agent drives tactical execution, nearly doubled the in-silico hit rate of a scientist working alone while uncovering hits across a much broader range of target sites. To scale wet-lab screening alongside our computational pipeline, we operationalized yeast surface display with fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS), a workflow that allows us to screen large libraries of engineered protein variants in parallel by fluorescence.

Our next step is to weave these threads together, combining VERID’s fully traceable automation with closed-loop learning for protein discovery to enable agents to directly navigate complex, rugged biological search spaces in the wet lab.

Safety

In line with Google’s Frontier Safety Framework and our approach to bioresilience, we build safeguards across both the computational and wet-lab sides of our workflows:

  • Safe testbeds and screening: We deliberately selected well-controlled, non-infectious biological systems without gain-of-function risk, as testbeds to evaluate agent behavior and catch drift early. Every designed sequence goes through biosecurity screening.
  • Simulation before execution: Through VERID, agents never send unverified code directly to the liquid handling robots. Every protocol is dry-run in simulation and validated against the digital twin before touching reagents.
  • Human oversight: Humans directly authorize and review designed sequences, verify wet-lab protocols, and supervise robot runs.

As AI agents take on more of the design-test cycle, new safety and reliability challenges emerge. Moving toward an autonomous wet lab requires solving these open problems with opportunities for human agency and oversight: ensuring agents optimize for true target binding rather than unintended experimental shortcuts, verifying multi-step wet-lab protocols, and continuously monitoring agent reasoning and execution traces.

From grounding agents in physical lab robotics, to running fast closed-loop aptamer cycles where agents learn to explore sequence space, to discovering single-digit nanomolar protein binders, these efforts form the building blocks for human-directed autonomous discovery in the life sciences. We're excited by this progress and look forward to sharing what comes next.

When we introduced Google Earth AI, we shared a suite of geospatial foundation models — spanning remote sensing, weather, flood hydrology, and population dynamics — alongside an initial prototype showing how a Gemini-powered agent could connect those models to answer cross-modal questions.

Since then, we have evolved a Geospatial Reasoning agent from an early concept into a much more capable, experimental system built for multi-step, geospatial reasoning across planet-scale data and autonomous training of custom predictive models. Today, we are sharing three updates:

  1. A new technical report on geospatial reasoning: We present systematic evaluations across four benchmarks, including GeoKTools and GeoExpertQueries, two new benchmarks we developed and are releasing for researchers to test their own geospatial reasoning agents. Our results quantify the value of Earth AI’s specialized tools and planning over out-of-the-box LLMs.
  2. Insights from real-world partner testing: Over the past few months, we invited a small group of social impact and commercial partner organizations — including the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Africa, People in Need, GiveDirectly, the Milken Institute and WPP — to test the agent in support of their own real-world workflows, such as disease outbreak investigations, disaster preparedness, and clean energy screening.
  3. Expanding early access on Google Earth and Google Cloud: We are expanding experimental access for both multi-step geospatial analysis and for planetary prediction. We’re offering early access to an experimental deep research update for Ask Google Earth. We’re also providing early access to an agent-to-agent API for developers building custom workflows, including integration recipes for connecting to Gemini.

What’s new in Geospatial Reasoning

General-purpose LLMs and standard coding tools struggle with real-world spatial problems because planetary datasets are massive, with specialized map and satellite formats that require careful multi-step planning to combine accurately. To tackle complex spatial workflows in practice, our agent brings together four key capabilities:

Connected to Earth AI foundation models and planet-scale data

The agent connects Gemini to the capabilities of Earth AI’s foundation models — including WeatherNext, Flood Forecasting, the Population Dynamics Foundation Model (PDFM), AlphaEarth Foundations and Remote Sensing Foundations — alongside information from Google Maps Platform (e.g., place information, routing, air quality, rooftop solar potential), Google Earth Engine, Data Commons and Google Dataset Search.

Modular skills, upfront planning and a dedicated spatial workspace

Earth AI capabilities are packaged as modular skills that the agent calls only when a user question needs them. Before running complex operations, the agent builds a step-by-step analytical plan, selects appropriate fallback datasets when local coverage is sparse, and processes large map layers in a dedicated workspace. This approach avoids overwhelming the agent context with massive amounts of spatial data, while preserving accuracy and tracking data attribution. Every response shows the agent’s plan and the data sources used so experts can check assumptions or substitute datasets.

Bring your own data

Organizations rarely rely on public data alone. Users can now input their own datasets via the Geospatial Reasoning agent API as CSV spreadsheets, custom map boundaries (GeoJSON), or cloud tables. Users can then ask the agent to join their private locations with Earth AI’s global models and catalogs.

From multi-step reasoning to autonomous Planetary Prediction

Beyond answering complex analytical questions, the agent also powers our recently announced Planetary Prediction Engine. Given a user’s local outcome data, such as regional disease rates, crop yields, or grid outages, the agent automatically selects relevant population and environmental signals, uses our Population Dynamics Insights and the annual Satellite Embedding dataset (Google products built on PDFM and AlphaEarth Foundations, respectively) and trains validated machine learning models for spatial prediction, super-resolution downscaling, and forecasting. In our recent public health research, combining these population and satellite signals improved predictions of health outcomes by 12% over demographic baselines and enabled mapping at 8X finer spatial resolution.

Our Geospatial Reasoning agent responds to a user’s question by first planning a multistep workflow, then selecting key Earth AI tools, datasets and models that are relevant to the query, and finally executing each stage of the plan in a workspace outside the context window. The answer incorporates multiple Earth AI capabilities into a text, tabular and map-based report.

Evaluating a Geospatial Reasoning agent

To measure the impact of domain-specific tools and upfront planning on geospatial reasoning, our technical report compares four agent configurations across Gemini 3.8 Flash and Gemini 3.1 Pro: (1) a standalone LLM, (2) the LLM with basic web search and maps grounding tools, (3) the LLM with Earth AI tools (such as Remote Sensing Foundations and WeatherNext 3) but without upfront planning, and (4) the full Geospatial Reasoning agent which begins every query with a dedicated planning stage that reasons over available capabilities to assess what it can and cannot do and sets out the stages of retrieval and processing needed to reach an answer.

We evaluate four agent configurations, from the base Gemini model, to agents progressively augmented with skills and orchestration that are optimized for geospatial reasoning.

The evaluation spans four benchmarks, covering expert-level open-ended analysis, multi-tool orchestration, and community-developed geospatial problems with deterministic answers. CBGB and UnivEARTH are two externally developed benchmarks that test geospatial code generation and question answering respectively. To test agents on challenging tasks that go beyond a single question or use case, we developed two new benchmarks. GeoExpertQueries introduces complex, real-world queries with expert-authored golden workflows that capture analysis best practices in domains like crisis resilience, site selection and public health. GeoKTools contains templated queries with verifiable answers, each requiring correct selection and use of 1 to 4 distinct geospatial tools. Together, this suite provides substantially broader coverage than prior evaluations of geospatial reasoning systems. To accelerate research and development of geospatial agents, we release the development splits of both our new benchmarks in full.

Example queries from our new GeoKTools (left) and GeoExpertQueries (right) benchmarks. GeoKTools tests an agent’s ability to select and use specific geospatial tools and datasets while GeoExpertQueries evaluates reasoning on open-ended, multi-step workflows.

Results and key takeaways

Two key takeaways stand out from our evaluation: First, domain-specific skills are essential for spatial reasoning. The agent with only basic tools (web search, maps grounding and code execution) struggles on quantitative spatial tasks. Equipping the agent with Earth AI skills drives a significant jump across GeoExpertQueries, GeoKTools, and CBGB. The only exception is UnivEARTH, where even a standalone LLM scores 93.6%, likely because the source NASA articles and answers are available on the public web.

Second, upfront planning unlocks open-ended, real-world workflows. While Earth AI skills alone are enough for narrower tasks like those in CBGB and GeoKTools, tackling open-ended problems in GeoExpertQueries requires upfront planning to keep the agent on track across multi-step analyses and prevent it from making unreliable assumptions or taking shortcuts like using web-search instead of spatial tools.

The table below shows scores across all four benchmarks using Gemini 3.8 Flash:

Scores are 0–100, averaged over three runs. Each benchmark is scored differently, so compare within a row, not across rows.

The technical report also discusses limitations. GeoExpertQueries scores come from an autorater that compares the agent’s performance to expert workflows that define the steps an analysis should take, not the correct final answer. We therefore consider the agent’s output as a strong first draft for experts to review and build on, not a final answer.

Earth AI in action: Early testing with partners

To evaluate how this research translates to real-world challenges, we gave a small group of partners early access to test the experimental agent on their toughest problems. Across public health, disaster response, and infrastructure planning, below is an overview of how they are putting Earth AI into action:

  • World Health Organization (WHO AFRO) & DRC’s INRB: At the start of the 2026 Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), WHO AFRO’s Emergency Preparedness and Response Hub in Dakar used the Geospatial Reasoning agent to map remote mining corridors where the exposure risk and human mobility are high by cross-referencing forest loss (from satellite images), mining sites (from maps and web data), and population data. In minutes, the team pinpointed 48 exposed settlements and located more than 45,500 at-risk people — a process that normally would have taken weeks. This allowed local responders to proactively deploy mobile laboratories and coordinate border surveillance. Meanwhile, the Epidemic Modeling and Intelligence Unit (UMIE) at the DRC’s National Institute for Biomedical Research (INRB) used the Planetary Prediction Engine to estimate the risk of Ebola spreading into uninfected zones. By combining mobility flows with historical case trends and Earth AI models and datasets, these weekly insights give coordinators critical planning time before cases arrive.
    • “Mobile populations like miners move faster than traditional paper surveillance can track, creating dangerous blind spots. Earth AI fills those gaps with satellite and mobility signals—moving us from reactively chasing a virus to actively forecasting where it will strike next.” Dr Etien Koua, HIS Program Area Manager & Hub Coordinator for WHO AFRO Emergency Preparedness and Response (watch the video)

  • People in Need: Geospatial reasoning helped combine natural disaster forecasts with population and imagery information, shifting analysts’ focus from data processing to providing insights:
    • "The experimental Geospatial Reasoning agent helped us analyze 14 historical cyclone paths to identify high-exposure villages in minutes rather than days of manual GIS work, turning prepared complex data into immediate insights and freeing up critical time for life-saving anticipatory action." - Alonso Gonzales, GIS and Remote Sensing Coordinator

  • GiveDirectly: Teams uploaded custom map boundaries to rapidly calculate population exposure by wind-speed zones during Tropical Cyclone Maila and benchmark tornado damage in Mississippi, cutting crisis scoping from days to minutes inside a single workspace.

  • WPP: Used geospatial reasoning to connect Population Dynamics Insights with their proprietary data. Their case study demonstrates how Earth AI insights enhanced the performance of geospatial marketing campaigns, while preserving the privacy of their data.

  • Milken Institute: Pre-development teams used the agent to combine their own lists of 1,500+ candidate buildings with Google Maps Platform’s Solar API and census data in order to screen locations for building community resilience hubs, taking into account rooftop solar potential, mobility data, nearby transit hubs, climate risks, and federal investment zone eligibility.

Watch the film

Link to Youtube Video

Early testing with these partners helped our evaluation and expansion of the agent’s geospatial skills, driving our recent additions of road-network routing, support for larger user-uploaded datasets, and better discovery of authoritative local data sources.

Expanding early access: Where you apply to test it

Today, we are expanding access across our Earth AI research capabilities to gather more feedback on these experimental geospatial reasoning capabilities. We are making these available to a limited group of early users:

  • Ask Google Earth: preview expanded deep analysis capabilities directly inside Ask Google Earth. This provides an interactive chat experience where you can ask complex spatial questions in natural language, analyze data — including your own — in Google Earth projects, and explore visual results directly on the map.
  • Geospatial Reasoning Agent API: For developer teams that want a customizable, do-it-yourself integration to power custom workflows, we offer an experimental headless Agent-to-Agent(A2A) service. Early partners can connect the Geospatial Reasoning agent to their own custom agents and data pipelines. We provide step-by-step developer recipes for teams who want to connect the service to their Gemini for business environment.

Our Planetary Prediction Engine capabilities are also available for early preview — accessible both through an interactive interface for rapid, plain-language modeling and via the Agent API for custom workflows.

To express interest in getting access to these research capabilities, please complete our interest form. To be among the first to try out our early stage projects, you can also sign up for our Early Access Pool.

We are living through a golden age of research and scientific discovery. For the scientists and researchers at Google Research, the opportunity extends beyond pioneering breakthroughs. We’re also building and sharing robust tools that empower the global ecosystem. AI acts as an amplifier of human ingenuity, creating the conditions for curiosity and rigorous inquiry to flourish.

Today, at our Research@ event in Mountain View, we are demonstrating how we put never-before-possible insights and capabilities into the hands of doctors, scientists, developers, public health officials, and others.

Here are 10 highlights:

1. Google Earth AI enables planetary intelligence for organizations and society

Addressing global challenges requires accurate, real-world planetary intelligence. With Google Earth AI, it becomes possible to forecast public health threats, accelerate clean energy investments, provide businesses with foresight, and more. Today, we’re expanding early access and inviting partners to explore three new ways to access Google Earth AI’s new, experimental capabilities:

  • Conducting deeper geospatial analysis as part of an early access experimental feature in Google Earth.
  • Generating risk assessments and forecasting different scenarios via our planetary prediction engine.
  • Integrating our Geospatial Reasoning agent skills directly into custom workflows via an experimental agent-to-agent API, provides developers with programmatic access to core features like satellite imagery parsing, routing and demographic embeddings.

We’re also announcing the integration of Google Dataset Search for querying from more than 100 million public datasets, and TimesFM for planetary nowcasting and forecasting iterations. All these capabilities are powered by over 70 geospatial tools including planetary foundation models like Remote Sensing Foundation Model (RSFM) and Population Dynamics Foundation Model (PDFM). They are validated by empirical benchmarks detailed in today’s Earth AI Technical Report. They enable developers, health leaders and enterprise teams to automate complex geospatial workflows.

To further support social impact efforts, Google.org is providing $10 million in funding to organizations working on crisis resilience and public health. This includes $2 million to The Milken Institute to unlock infrastructure bottlenecks for affordable housing, clean energy, broadband, safe water systems, and other essential infrastructure.

Google Earth AI’s geospatial foundation models are being used to help predict disease outbreaks and enable public health teams to take proactive, preventive action.

2. Multi-agent orchestration helps scientists build on existing knowledge

Existing literature offers a great source of knowledge for driving new scientific discoveries. We built a multi-agent orchestrator, enabling scientists to reproduce previous methods and analyses and then apply them in new settings to tackle important research challenges. As an example, this helped researchers apply a new methodology for solving inverse design problems in fluid mechanics to the design of urinary catheters. They discovered catheter designs that, in simulation, were better at preventing bacterial infections.

This complements our existing tools to accelerate scientific workflows. Empirical Research Assistance enables scientists to generate and test thousands of code variations in parallel, and has helped researchers produce results from biology to cosmology to economics. Co-Scientist, built in collaboration with Google DeepMind, is a multi-agent tool that can generate novel hypotheses and has already helped partners, like researchers at Stanford University, uncover repurposed medicines to fight liver fibrosis.

3. Deep Review helps authors improve the clarity and accuracy of technical documents

Thorough peer review is a core part of the scientific method. We created Deep Review, an agentic system that provides rigorous verification across complex documents. This is particularly important as AI is increasingly being used to help experts draft technical documents. Many Google researchers and external authors have already used an early version of this system to review over 16,000 research publications submitted to top-tier computer science conferences. It helps with the heavy cognitive lifting by checking logical consistency and grounding facts, while scientists maintain authority over creative direction. Today, we’re expanding access to Deep Review to the general public to help people verify a variety of technical documents from legal agreements to financial reports.

System architecture showing the four-stage pipeline.

4. Next-gen Edge AI chip enables manufacturers to build the wearables of tomorrow

With the rise of wearable devices, hardware manufacturers need the tools to develop efficient edge applications to meet the high expectations of customers for all-day performance. Earlier this year, we launched the first Coralboard from Synaptics, using Google’s Coral NPU accelerator core. It enables AI and ML engineers to rapidly prototype and build devices. On October 20th, Synaptics launched the Synaptics Astra SR200 Series, their next-gen, low power Edge AI chip, which includes our co-designed open source Coral NPU. The chip delivers greater efficiency and performance for design engineers building the next generation of smart glasses and watches, connected cameras, streamers, and industrial vision and voice systems.

The new low-power Edge AI chip from Synaptics, as displayed next to a coin for its relative size.

5. TimesFM and TabFM transform how businesses work with numbers

While language models excel with text, business and operational decisions also rely on numbers. TimesFM and TabFM are foundational models engineered specifically to reason over raw numerical distributions — time-series streams (data that changes over time) and structured tabular data (like spreadsheets). Both models deliver accurate predictions out of the box with zero training. They rank at the top of leading public benchmarks in their fields and are available to all Cloud BigQuery users. Today, we are announcing our upcoming integration of these models into Gemini for business. Soon, business owners, analysts, operation leads or coordinators can forecast trends like product sales or hospital bed capacity, based on complex operational tables and millions of rows of data. Sensitive data stays safely within an organization’s perimeter, and people get the answers they need in seconds.

TimesFM-3's multivariate forecast helps to anticipate sales lift for a business on planned promotion days in the future.

6. MedGemma enables innovators to build and deploy health AI applications

MedGemma, published last week in Nature Medicine, has been downloaded more than 10 million times by more than 65,000 unique innovators. It serves as an open foundation for developers building specialized applications. Developers have adapted it to meet the needs of their local communities, from enabling faster triage in overcrowded clinics to screening for eye disease and cervical cancer.

As developers fine-tune MedGemma for more specialities and care settings, we’re pushing the frontier of open health AI. Our latest research advances MedGemma with tool use, so it can draw on available health records and other applications clinicians rely on. We’re exploring new modalities like mammography, ultrasound and electrocardiograms. Early signs point to substantial gains in capabilities, such as answering clinical questions and interpreting radiology scans, skin images and pathology slides. items.content:
Generative AI has accelerated many technical fields. It is now common for AI to play some role in writing scientific papers and technical documents, running code, designing experiments, and drafting proposals. However, accelerating content creation has created a review challenge: the human capacity for verification has remained largely fixed amid this rapid increase in AI-generated content. Reviewing complex documents like long scientific manuscripts or complex legal agreements requires specialized expertise and advanced subject knowledge. This imbalance creates a validation bottleneck, where information is being generated faster than it can be rigorously reviewed.

Today, we’re excited to announce the public release of Deep Review, an agentic AI system engineered to provide rigorous feedback and technical verification on complex documents. Initially designed for computer science academic paper analysis, the system’s capabilities have expanded to review documents across many domains, such as legal and finance. It can be used as both an iterative improvement tool during the drafting process and a tool for the scientific process verification, claims, and evaluation during the review process.

Deep Review represents the evolution of our Paper Assistant Tool (PAT) — an experimental initiative developed to help researchers stress-test manuscripts prior to conference submission. Over the past year, we partnered with four flagship computer science conferences (STOC 2026, ICML 2026, NeurIPS 2026, and ICLR 2027) to provide private, pre-submission feedback to authors of more than 16,000 manuscripts who opted in. Further details on PAT and these pilots can be found in our manuscript, Towards Automating Scientific Review with Google’s Paper Assistant Tool.

With this release, Deep Review is now accessible worldwide:

  • Tiered access and scalable API: Every user receives two complimentary document reviews per week. Users with high-volume workflows can connect their Gemini API key for higher usage limits and programmatic integration via the Deep Review API.
  • Format flexibility: Deep Review will initially support PDFs and plain text as input formats, with support for multi-file inputs coming soon.
  • Privacy and data policy: Documents uploaded to Deep Review are never used to train, fine-tune, or improve Google models. Uploaded documents are stored for one year for the sole purpose of display to the user in the Deep Review UI.

Deep Review accelerates technical validation

One of the most significant examples of the validation bottleneck is in academic peer review. This can be seen in the uptick of submissions to academic publication venues, especially venues for AI research itself, which have seen a dramatic rise. This year, there were over 74,000 submissions to three major AI conferences (ICLR, NeurIPS, and ICML) up from approximately 45,000 in 2025, 32,000 in 2024, and 23,000 in 2023. Each of these submissions requires multiple high-quality reviews to ensure the integrity of the peer review process, which can place a larger burden on human experts.

Increase in submissions to NeurIPS, ICML, and ICLR between 2023 and 2026.

Deep Review aims to help alleviate this expanding burden on human reviewers across technical fields. By providing detailed, objective evaluations of documents, Deep Review checks logical consistency and mathematical statements, suggests improvements, grounds facts, and compares with existing work. It addresses some of the most cognitively burdensome facets of review, while leaving higher-level judgements to humans.

A proven track record for scientific review

Deep Review has been extensively tested and deployed under its experimental name, the Paper Assistant Tool (PAT), in four pilot partnerships with the flagship computer science conferences STOC 2026, ICML 2026, NeurIPS 2026, and ICLR 2027. During these pilots, authors were able to opt-in to receive feedback and analysis on their paper via PAT in the weeks before the submission deadline. The goal was to provide authors with actionable feedback to help improve the quality of papers in submission. This feedback was completely decoupled from the official conference review process. PAT did not collect any of the data for training, and papers were deleted from Google systems promptly after each program concluded.

Author reactions to the tool have been extremely positive, and reflect continued improvements to both underlying models and the PAT harness. With the addition of Gemini 4 Argon support in Deep Review, the underlying capabilities of the tool have further increased beyond the older iterations of PAT described below.

Statistics and author feedback from the pilot programs of PAT at machine learning and theoretical computer science conferences.

How Deep Review works

Single-prompt LLM calls often fail when evaluating long, complex documents due to exhausting their token reasoning budget, overlooking long-context cross-section dependencies, or accepting nuanced claims without fully scrutinizing them. Deep Review solves these challenges through a four-stage agentic pipeline:

  1. Document segmentation: The document is first ingested and autonomously decomposed by a segmenter agent into logical segments (e.g., Introduction, experiments, methodology, etc.). These segments can be overlapping, and must cover all the content of the input document.
  2. Adaptive budgeting: Not all sections require equal cognitive depth. The pipeline inspects information density and dynamically allocates a compute budget, along with a specialized inference scaling pipeline for each section. For instance, sections with dense mathematical proofs may receive more compute than an introduction or a related work section in an academic paper.
  3. Deep parallel verification: Specialized reasoning agents scrutinize each segment in parallel. Each agent has access to the full document context to track cross-references, but focuses its reasoning power specifically on the task of reviewing its specific target section. This ensures both that reviewing tasks are manageable for each review swarm, and that parallel swarms are properly coordinated.
  4. Global synthesis and agentic grounding: A dedicated synthesis agent consolidates the segment-level reports, and does final consistency checks between sections, rerunning logical checks if required. The agent further performs external grounding checks and tool calls as a final preventative measure against hallucinations.

System architecture showing the four-stage pipeline.

Universal verification and review: Beyond research papers

While Deep Review originated in academic paper reviews, long-context review is generalizable: reasoning mechanisms used to check whether a mathematical proof holds up in a research paper can also help surface logical gaps and inconsistencies in other types of documents, where claims must be backed by evidence. Therefore, Deep Review can be used to bring structured critique to a broader range of everyday workflows.

Users can now apply Deep Review to analyze complex documents across many domains. For instance, it can be run on:

  • Design documents: Catch unstated architectural assumptions, spot edge cases, and suggest concrete improvements.
  • Presentations: Ensure slide transitions flow logically and bulleted takeaways match visual charts.
  • Legal and financial documents: Check internal consistency across clauses and data tables, flag ambiguous terms or downstream consequences, and ground claims against supporting evidence.

Deep Review meets Antigravity

We’re also introducing the Teamwork Deep Document Review Pattern, a document review implementation pattern inspired by Deep Review built into Antigravity using the Teamwork multi-agent orchestration framework. This pattern is designed systematically to evaluate research papers, manuscript drafts, and technical proposals using a multi-agent hierarchy with self-correction and segment-based rubrics. Antigravity users can invoke this pattern using the /teamwork-preview command.

Making thorough, high-quality technical reviews widely accessible

Comprehensive pre-submission critique in computer science has generally depended on access to extensive review networks — like senior faculty, well-resourced academic laboratories, or extensive peer advisory networks. Providing reliable, automated logical verification can help many academics stress-test their assertions, identify avoidable flaws, refine and strengthen their documents based on verified foundations, and present their work in a review process with more confidence.

Get started

We invite researchers, engineers, and creators everywhere to explore Deep Review:

  • Try Deep Review: Visit the Google Research Portal to review your first documents.
  • Integrate with the API: Access programmatic verification in your continuous integration and drafting workflows using your Gemini API key.
  • Read the research: Read the preprint to explore the underlying methodology and pilot evaluations.

Conclusion and looking ahead

Given the utility it demonstrated during our pilot programs with academic conferences, we believe that tools like Deep Review will play a significant role across the peer review process in the coming years by empowering both authors and reviewers.

Moving forward, we are continuing to expand the platform’s capabilities. With the rollout of Gemini 4 Argon support, Deep Review’s underlying capabilities further improve, delivering even higher quality feedback and analysis to authors. Additionally, with multi-file support coming soon, users will also be able to run these same consistency checks across entire sets of related documents, spreadsheets, and exhibits simultaneously. We hope these advancements will make high-quality technical reviews more widely accessible for knowledge workers everywhere.

Acknowledgments

Deep Review is a collaborative effort across Google Research, Google DeepMind, and Google Cloud. We thank our core contributors and research collaborators — Santiago Balseiro, Taylan Cemgil, Tommaso D'Orsi, Kirk Draheim, Lindi Emoungu, Ayse Erduran, Palash Goyal, Caroline Hartnell, Shobana Kannan, Amy Keeling, Siyi Kou, Bridget Lee, Ian Li, Anoushka Mazumdar, Taylor Montgomery, Mouad Naciri, Uche Okonkwo, Mihir Parmar, Anthony Phalen, Rory Pilgrim, Sarah Presotto Post, Rob Tierney, Drew Tyler, Vishnu V., Vahab Mirrokni, Laura Vardoulakis, Johannes Welbl, David Woodruff, Yunhan Xu, Jinsung Yoon — as well as our executive sponsors Katherine Chou, Corinna Cortes, Burak Gokturk, Vahab Mirrokni, Tomas Pfister, Yossi Matias and the Program Chairs of STOC, ICML, NeurIPS, and ICLR for their partnership.

Antigravity users can invoke this pattern using the /teamwork-preview command.
Making thorough, high-quality technical reviews widely accessible
Comprehensive pre-submission critique in computer science has generally depended on access to extensive review networks — like senior faculty, well-resourced academic laboratories, or extensive peer advisory networks. Providing reliable, automated logical verification can help many academics stress-test their assertions, identify avoidable flaws, refine and strengthen their documents based on verified foundations, and present their work in a review process with more confidence.
Get started
We invite researchers, engineers, and creators everywhere to explore Deep Review:

Try Deep Review: Visit the Google Research Portal to review your first documents.
Integrate with the API: Access programmatic verification in your continuous integration and drafting workflows using your Gemini API key.
Read the research: Read the preprint to explore the underlying methodology and pilot evaluations.

  



    
Conclusion and looking ahead
Given the utility it demonstrated during our pilot programs with academic conferences, we believe that tools like Deep Review will play a significant role across the peer review process in the coming years by empowering both authors and reviewers.
Moving forward, we are continuing to expand the platform’s capabilities. With the rollout of Gemini 4 Argon support, Deep Review’s underlying capabilities further improve, delivering even higher quality feedback and analysis to authors. Additionally, with multi-file support coming soon, users will also be able to run these same consistency checks across entire sets of related documents, spreadsheets, and exhibits simultaneously. We hope these advancements will make high-quality technical reviews more widely accessible for knowledge workers everywhere.

summaries.zh: Deep Review 是一款由 Google 开发的 AI 系统，用于对复杂文档进行严格的反馈和技术验证，支持科学、法律、金融等领域。该系统最初为计算机科学学术论文分析设计，现已全球发布，提供每周两次免费文档评审，并可通过 API 进行扩展。Deep Review 可在起草过程中迭代改进，或在评审阶段验证科学声明。系统基于实验性 Paper Assistant Tool (PAT) 发展，已与四大计算机会议合作，为 16,000 多篇论文提供预提交反馈。Deep Review 支持 PDF 和纯文本格式输入，上传文档仅用于展示，不用于模型训练。
summaries.en: Deep Review is an agentic AI system designed to rigorously review complex technical documents, addressing the bottleneck created by AI-generated content outpacing human review capacity. Initially developed for computer science papers, it now supports legal and finance documents, offering iterative improvement and verification tools. Launched publicly, it provides feedback on logical consistency, mathematical statements, and comparisons with existing work,减轻 the burden on human reviewers. Deep Review evolved from the Paper Assistant Tool (PAT), which was tested in partnerships with major conferences, analyzing over 16,000 manuscripts. It offers tiered access, supports PDF and plain text inputs, and ensures user data privacy.
